**Surah al-Inshirah (Opening Up) is Meccan and has eight verses.**

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Did We not open up your breast for you?﴾ ﴿And We removed from you your burden,﴾ ﴿which had weighed down your back?﴾ ﴿And We raised high your remembrance.﴾ ﴿So indeed, with hardship comes ease.﴾ ﴿Indeed, with hardship comes ease.﴾ ﴿So when you are free, then strive hard,﴾ ﴿and to your Lord turn with longing.﴾

This surah is Meccan, and its connection to what precedes it is evident. "Opening up the breast" (sharh al-sadr) means illuminating it with wisdom and widening it to receive what is revealed to him. This is the view of the majority. The better view is that the expression is general, covering this and other things, such as bearing the hardship of calling to God alone and enduring the hostility of the unbelievers' harm. Ibn 'Abbas and a group of scholars said that it refers to Gabriel (peace be upon him) splitting open the Prophet's breast in his childhood.

The interrogative hamza (hamzat al-istifham, the question particle) entered upon a negation, which conveys affirmation of this blessing. The meaning is: "We have indeed opened your breast for you." For this reason, the past-tense verb "We placed" (wada'na) is coordinated with it. This is similar to God's words: ﴿Did We not raise you among us as a child, and did you not remain among us for years?﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 18].

The majority read (nashrah) with a jussive vowel on the ha' because of the entry of the jussive particle. Abu Ja'far read it with a fatha on the ha'. Ibn 'Atiyya, in his book, explained this as the original form *alam nashrahan*, in which the nun was changed to an alif, and then the alif was deleted for lightness. This is like what Abu Zayd recited in his *Nawadir* from the words of the rajaz poet:

*From which of my two days of death do I flee: the day not decreed, or the day that was decreed?*

And another poet said:

*I strike away from you the cares that knock at you, a blow with the sword to the crest of the horse.*

Abu Hayyan said: this is a rejected reading (qira'a mardhulah). Al-Zamakhshari mentioned it from Abu Ja'far al-Mansur, and they said: perhaps he made the ha' clear and prolonged it in its place of articulation, so the listener thought he had pronounced it with a fatha. End of quote.

There is a better explanation for this reading than all of this: it is a dialect of some Arabs, related by al-Lihyani in his *Nawadir*. In it, the jussive is used with *lan* and the subjunctive with *lam*, the reverse of what is known among people. He recited the words of 'A'isha bint al-A'jam praising al-Mukhtar ibn Abi 'Ubayd, who avenged al-Husayn ibn 'Ali (may God be pleased with them both):

*The pillar of guidance had been crumbling, its support falling, until al-Mukhtar came to it and it stood firm.*

*In everything he resolved upon, he carried out his opinion boldly, and did not consult anyone in his undertaking.*

Here "*yushawira*" (he consult) is in the subjunctive. This explanation fits both interpretations and is better than what preceded it.

﴿And We removed from you your burden﴾ is a kinaya (a figurative expression, here meaning an implied reference) to his protection from sins and his purification from defilements. It is expressed as a removal in order to emphasise the negation of such things, just as one says: "I lifted from you the hardship of visiting," to one who never visited at all, emphasising the absence of visiting from him.

The lexicographers said: "*anqada al-himl zahr al-naqah*" means the load made the she-camel's back creak, when you hear a creaking from the intensity of the load. One also says "*sami'tu naqid al-mirjal*," meaning its creaking (the sound of a cooking pot). 'Abbas ibn Mirdas said:

*And what I bent under from them made my back creak, though I was caring for them, tender toward them.*

Jamil said:

*Until its ropes were pulled with a creak, and the beams of its frame were about to break apart.*

*Al-naqid* is the sound of breaking apart and coming loose.

﴿And We raised high your remembrance﴾ means that He linked his name with His own in the testimony of faith, in the call to prayer, in the iqamah (the second call to prayer), in the tashahhud (the testimony in prayer), and in the sermons. It also appears in other places in the Qur'an, in calling him "Prophet of God" and "Messenger of God," in his mention in the earlier scriptures, and in the covenant taken from the prophets and their peoples that they would believe in him. Hassan said:

*Upon him is the seal of prophethood, bright, from God, witnessed, shining and bearing witness.*

*God joined the name of the Prophet to His own name, when the muezzin says in the five prayers: "I bear witness."*

The enumeration of these blessings upon him (ﷺ) implies that just as God has been good to you with these ranks, He will be good to you by granting you victory over your enemies and helping you against them. The unbelievers also used to reproach the believers for their poverty, so He reminded him of these blessings and strengthened his hope by saying: ﴿So indeed, with hardship comes ease﴾, that is, with constriction comes relief. Then He repeated it for emphasis regarding the coming of ease. Since ease follows hardship without a long lapse of time, it is treated as if it were with it. In this is good news to the Messenger (ﷺ) that ease will come soon.

The apparent view is that the repetition is for emphasis, as we have said. It has also been said that the ease is repeated in terms of its location: there is ease in this world and ease in the Hereafter. It has also been said that with every hardship there are two eases, because the hardship is definite (*al-'usr*, with the article, referring to a known thing) while the ease is indefinite (*yusr*, without the article), so the first is other than the second. In a hadith: "Hardship will never overcome two eases."

Ibn Wththab, Abu Ja'far and 'Isa read the *sin* of (*al-'usr*) and (*yusran*) in these verses with a damma (*'usr*, *yusr*), while the majority read them with a sukun (silent vowel).

When God enumerated His earlier blessings upon him, and promised him to make easy what was hard for him, He commanded him to persevere in worship when he finished one act of worship and not to slacken. Ibn Mas'ud said: ﴿So when you are free﴾ from your obligation ﴿then strive hard﴾ in voluntary worship, as an act of devotion to your Lord. He also said: ﴿then strive hard﴾ in the night vigil. Mujahid said: "When you are free﴾ from the business of your worldly life ﴿then strive hard﴾ in the worship of your Lord. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: ﴿When you are free﴾ from the prayer ﴿then strive hard﴾ in supplication. Al-Hasan said: ﴿When you are free﴾ from jihad ﴿then strive hard﴾ in worship. The majority read (*fansab*) with a silent ba' and a light pronunciation, while some read it with a shadda and a fatha, from *al-insab* (to strive). Others among the Imamiyya read *fansib* with a kasra on the sad, meaning: "When you are free from the message, then appoint a successor (*khalifah*)." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is an anomalous reading, weak in meaning, and it has not been authenticated from any scholar." End of quote.

There is a better explanation for this reading than all of this: it is a dialect of some Arabs, related by al-Lihyani in his *Nawadir*. In it, the jussive is used with *lan* and the subjunctive with *lam*, the reverse of what is known among people. He recited the words of 'A'isha bint al-A'jam praising al-Mukhtar ibn Abi 'Ubayd, who avenged al-Husayn ibn 'Ali (may God be pleased with them both):

*The pillar of guidance had been crumbling, its support falling, until al-Mukhtar came to it and it stood firm.*

*In everything he resolved upon, he carried out his opinion boldly, and did not consult anyone in his undertaking.*

Here "*yushawira*" (he consult) is in the subjunctive. This explanation fits both interpretations and is better than what preceded it.

﴿And We removed from you your burden﴾ is a kinaya (a figurative expression, here meaning an implied reference) to his protection from sins and his purification from defilements. It is expressed as a removal in order to emphasise the negation of such things, just as one says: "I lifted from you the hardship of visiting," to one who never visited at all, emphasising the absence of visiting from him.

The lexicographers said: "*anqada al-himl zahr al-naqah*" means the load made the she-camel's back creak, when you hear a creaking from the intensity of the load. One also says "*sami'tu naqid al-mirjal*," meaning its creaking (the sound of a cooking pot). 'Abbas ibn Mirdas said:

*And what I bent under from them made my back creak, though I was caring for them, tender toward them.*

Jamil said:

*Until its ropes were pulled with a creak, and the beams of its frame were about to break apart.*

*Al-naqid* is the sound of breaking apart and coming loose.

﴿And We raised high your remembrance﴾ means that He linked his name with His own in the testimony of faith, in the call to prayer, in the iqamah (the second call to prayer), in the tashahhud (the testimony in prayer), and in the sermons. It also appears in other places in the Qur'an, in calling him "Prophet of God" and "Messenger of God," in his mention in the earlier scriptures, and in the covenant taken from the prophets and their peoples that they would believe in him. Hassan said:

*Upon him is the seal of prophethood, bright, from God, witnessed, shining and bearing witness.*

*God joined the name of the Prophet to His own name, when the muezzin says in the five prayers: "I bear witness."*

The enumeration of these blessings upon him (ﷺ) implies that just as God has been good to you with these ranks, He will be good to you by granting you victory over your enemies and helping you against them. The unbelievers also used to reproach the believers for their poverty, so He reminded him of these blessings and strengthened his hope by saying: ﴿So indeed, with hardship comes ease﴾, that is, with constriction comes relief. Then He repeated it for emphasis regarding the coming of ease. Since ease follows hardship without a long lapse of time, it is treated as if it were with it. In this is good news to the Messenger (ﷺ) that ease will come soon.

The apparent view is that the repetition is for emphasis, as we have said. It has also been said that the ease is repeated in terms of its location: there is ease in this world and ease in the Hereafter. It has also been said that with every hardship there are two eases, because the hardship is definite (*al-'usr*, with the article, referring to a known thing) while the ease is indefinite (*yusr*, without the article), so the first is other than the second. In a hadith: "Hardship will never overcome two eases."

Ibn Wththab, Abu Ja'far and 'Isa read the *sin* of (*al-'usr*) and (*yusran*) in these verses with a damma (*'usr*, *yusr*), while the majority read them with a sukun (silent vowel).

When God enumerated His earlier blessings upon him, and promised him to make easy what was hard for him, He commanded him to persevere in worship when he finished one act of worship and not to slacken. Ibn Mas'ud said: ﴿So when you are free﴾ from your obligation ﴿then strive hard﴾ in voluntary worship, as an act of devotion to your Lord. He also said: ﴿then strive hard﴾ in the night vigil. Mujahid said: "When you are free﴾ from the business of your worldly life ﴿then strive hard﴾ in the worship of your Lord. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: ﴿When you are free﴾ from the prayer ﴿then strive hard﴾ in supplication. Al-Hasan said: ﴿When you are free﴾ from jihad ﴿then strive hard﴾ in worship. This statement of his is objected to, since jihad was made obligatory in Medina.

The majority read ﴿faraghta﴾ (you are free) with a fatha on the ra', while Abu al-Sammal read it with a kasra, which is a dialect. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is not eloquent." The majority read (*fansab*) with a silent ba' and a light pronunciation, while some read it with a shadda and a fatha, from *al-insab* (to strive). Others among the Imamiyya read *fansib* with a kasra on the sad, meaning: "When you are free from the message, then appoint a successor (*khalifah*)." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is an anomalous reading, weak in meaning, and it has not been authenticated from any scholar." End of quote.

The majority read ﴿farghab﴾ (turn with longing), an imperative from *raghiba* in its triliteral form, meaning: direct the aspiration of desires toward Him alone, not toward anything else. Zayd ibn 'Ali and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read *fargghib*, an imperative from *raghghaba* with a shadda on the ghayn.
